Autoregressive video prediction models generate frames sequentially, each conditioned on some window of previously generated frames — so errors in early frames get fed back as inputs, and the model must extrapolate from its own (imperfect) outputs rather than ground-truth data. The central question is: how does the distribution of generated frames drift away from the true data distribution as rollout length increases, and what structural properties of the model or conditioning scheme either accelerate or dampen that drift? The key concepts are compounding error (small per-step residuals that multiply across time), exposure bias (the train/test mismatch between conditioning on real vs. generated frames), and the spectral properties of the recurrent operator — specifically whether repeated application contracts or expands variation in the latent or pixel space. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is not the obvious catastrophic collapse (blurry video, obvious artifacts) but the subtle drift: a model that looks perceptually fine at frame 100 but has silently migrated to a statistically distinct manifold — wrong object permanence, violated physical constraints, shifted color statistics — in ways that standard FVD or PSNR metrics fail to catch because those metrics don't measure distributional consistency over time. The expert also worries about the interaction between the context window size and drift rate: truncating the conditioning window can prevent error accumulation but severs long-range temporal coherence, while extending it risks the model learning to "trust" its own hallucinations.

Standard metrics like FVD (Fréchet Video Distance) and PSNR fail here for a structural reason: they measure marginal frame quality or short-clip statistics against a reference distribution, but they are insensitive to conditional consistency — whether frame t+k is plausible given frame t, not just plausible in isolation. A proper drift-detection protocol needs to measure at minimum three things: (1) temporal autocorrelation decay — how quickly statistical dependencies between frames fall off compared to real video, which would catch a model that generates locally coherent but globally amnesiac sequences; (2) physical invariant violation rates — tracking whether conserved quantities like object identity, approximate mass/volume, and scene topology remain stable across hundreds of frames, similar to what PhyDNet and related physics-constrained models use as training signals but applied here as eval probes; and (3) distributional shift under re-encoding — run the generated video through an encoder trained only on real data and track the trajectory of latent codes over time; a drifting model will show a systematic walk away from the real-data manifold rather than stationary fluctuation around it. The latent trajectory test is particularly sharp because it can quantify drift rate (e.g., Wasserstein distance between the latent distribution at frames 1–30 vs. frames 271–300) and distinguish directional drift from mere increased variance. What makes this hard is that you need long rollout test sets — on the order of 300–1000 frames — which almost no standard benchmark provides; Kinetics clips top out at ~250 frames, and most video generation benchmarks (UCF-101 eval, Something-Something) use clips under 5 seconds. The deeper reason standard metrics miss this is that they were designed to evaluate generators against a fixed dataset, not to evaluate dynamical systems for stability — a category error that mirrors the mistake of using image classifiers to evaluate video understanding.

Several concrete interventions have been proposed beyond scheduled sampling. DAgger-style online data aggregation (Ross et al., 2011, originally for imitation learning) directly addresses exposure bias by periodically rolling out the current model, collecting the resulting (imperfect) frames, and training on corrections from an expert policy — adapted to video, this means training on model-generated conditioning frames with ground-truth next-frame targets, forcing the model to learn recovery behavior from its own error modes rather than only from clean data. Contrastive or adversarial regularization on the dynamics — as explored in RSSM variants (Hafner et al., Dreamer series) and world model literature — trains a discriminator not on individual frame quality but on trajectory plausibility, penalizing the generator when its multi-step rollouts diverge statistically from real trajectories; this directly pressures the learned transition operator toward contractiveness. Spectral normalization of the recurrent core (Miyato et al., 2018, originally for GANs) can be applied to the temporal transition weights to explicitly bound the Lipschitz constant of the dynamics map, preventing the operator from having eigenvalues greater than 1 that would cause exponential error amplification — VideoGPT and similar transformer-based models could apply this to attention weight matrices over the temporal axis. The theoretical obstacle is sharp: contractiveness and expressiveness are in direct tension. A provably contractive dynamics model (all singular values of the Jacobian < 1) will damp not just errors but also genuine long-range signal — slow-moving objects, gradual lighting changes, sustained motion trajectories — because the model cannot distinguish "error to suppress" from "real low-frequency variation to preserve." This is formalized in the stability-expressiveness tradeoff studied in echo state networks and reservoir computing, where maximizing the spectral radius up to but not exceeding 1 (the "edge of chaos") is theoretically optimal but practically untrainable because the gradient landscape at that boundary is pathologically ill-conditioned.

Selective contractiveness is theoretically grounded in the idea of inertial manifolds from dynamical systems theory — the notion that high-dimensional dynamics often have a low-dimensional attracting manifold on which the true signal lives, with transverse directions (the error modes) being genuinely contractive. The practical question is whether a model can learn to decompose its latent space into "along-manifold" directions (preserve) and "off-manifold" directions (damp), which is exactly what slow feature analysis and its deep descendants attempt: SFA explicitly learns features that change slowly over time, which under stationarity assumptions corresponds to learning the signal subspace. More recently, keypoint-structured latent spaces (Transporter, Jakab et al. 2020; LEAP) do this implicitly by factoring video into slowly-varying structural variables (object positions, poses) and rapidly-varying appearance residuals — the structural variables get the expressive dynamics and the residuals are regularized toward zero, achieving selective contractiveness by architectural fiat rather than spectral constraint. The theoretical obstacle is that distinguishing error modes from signal modes requires the model to have a prior over what should change — essentially a model of the scene's causal structure — and during generation that prior must be applied without access to ground truth, creating a circular dependency: you need to know what's signal to damp what's noise, but you can only know what's signal if you're not already drifting. This is precisely why object-centric video models (SLATE, SAVi, Steve) show better long-rollout stability than monolithic models — by construction they separate "object persists with identity" (slow, preserved) from "pixel appearance given object" (fast, regularized) — but they pay a steep price in scenes that don't decompose cleanly into discrete objects, where the inductive bias becomes a straitjacket. The deepest issue is that "error mode" is not an intrinsic property of a direction in latent space but a contextual one — the same direction might be signal in one scene and noise in another — which means truly selective contractiveness requires something closer to online uncertainty estimation over latent directions, a problem that connects directly to Bayesian filtering but at the scale of modern video architectures where exact inference is intractable.

At topological boundaries, object-centric models face what might be called a slot assignment crisis: the discrete binding between slots and objects — which is the mechanism that enforces slow/fast factorization — must either be maintained through an occlusion event (requiring the model to track an invisible object) or broken and re-established (requiring it to recognize the same object post-occlusion as a continuation rather than a new entity). SAVi++ (Elsayed et al., 2022) explicitly studied this and found that tracking fidelity degrades sharply at occlusion boundaries, with slot identity swaps occurring in roughly 30–40% of occlusion events on complex scenes, and crucially these swaps are irreversible under autoregressive rollout — once a slot has been reassigned, the model has no mechanism to recover the original binding, so the error compounds rather than self-corrects. The drift pattern at these boundaries is characteristically discontinuous rather than gradual: rather than the slow manifold walk seen in non-topological drift, you get discrete jumps in latent space corresponding to slot permutation events, after which the model is effectively tracking a different scene than the one it started with — object permanence is violated, but the per-frame appearance loss may remain low if the substituted slot is visually plausible. Appearance discontinuities (a light switching on, a fast camera cut) are arguably worse because they invalidate the slow-feature assumption not just for one object but for the entire scene simultaneously, causing all slots to partially reset — in STEVE and SLATE, this manifests as a momentary spike in reconstruction error followed by re-binding to a new configuration that may not be semantically consistent with the pre-discontinuity state. What makes this particularly damaging for long rollouts is that natural video has a power-law distribution of scene complexity, meaning topological events are not rare edge cases but occur with roughly constant rate per unit time — in something like a cooking video, object merging (ingredients combining), occlusion (hand over bowl), and appearance change (heat browning food) happen every few seconds, so a model doing 300-frame rollout will encounter dozens of these crisis points. The underlying issue is that the inductive bias of object-centric models encodes a topological assumption — that the scene's object graph is stable — which is precisely the assumption that interesting, dynamic scenes violate most frequently, creating an inverse correlation between scene richness and model stability that no amount of training data can fully overcome without a fundamentally different treatment of discrete structural change.

The most principled internal detection signal is slot competition entropy: in well-functioning object-centric models, the attention weights that bind slots to spatial regions are typically low-entropy (each slot owns a distinct region), but at a topological boundary — occlusion onset, merge, appearance jump — multiple slots simultaneously compete for the same spatial evidence, producing a transient spike in attention entropy that is detectable without any ground truth reference. A second internal signal is slot velocity discontinuity: under normal slow-feature dynamics, slot representations change smoothly between frames, so an anomalous jump in the L2 distance between a slot's representation at t and t+1 — beyond what the model's own uncertainty estimate predicts — flags a potential binding crisis; this is essentially a Mahalanobis distance test against the model's learned transition prior, analogous to innovation monitoring in Kalman filtering. The corrective mechanism that detection should trigger is not a full re-initialization (which would discard all accumulated context) but a targeted slot reset with context retention: freeze the unaffected slots, re-run the binding attention for the flagged slot using an expanded spatial window, and re-anchor it to the post-boundary evidence while preserving its semantic history in a separate memory buffer — something architecturally close to what Neural Process-based video models attempt but not yet implemented in mainstream object-centric systems. The deep difficulty is false positive cost asymmetry: triggering correction on a non-crisis (e.g., fast but continuous motion) disrupts stable bindings and introduces exactly the slot permutation you were trying to prevent, while missing a true crisis allows irreversible drift — so the detection threshold is a high-stakes hyperparameter with no principled way to set it without rollout-length-specific calibration. This points to a broader gap: current object-centric models have no formal notion of confidence in their own topological state, which would require something like a discrete latent variable over scene graph structure whose posterior could be tracked — a direction explored in object-centric reinforcement learning (OCRL) but largely absent from video prediction, where the computational cost of maintaining a distribution over scene graphs at video frame rates remains prohibitive.

A compressed topological surprise signal is not only plausible but has partial precedents: free energy in predictive coding models (Friston et al.) and negative ELBO spikes in VAE-based video models both function as scalar surprises that aggregate evidence against the current model state, and in practice these do correlate with perceptual discontinuities — a VAE trained on video will show ELBO drops at cut boundaries, occlusion onsets, and appearance changes at rates meaningfully above baseline. The most natural compressed signal for slot-based models is a weighted sum of per-slot attention entropy and slot velocity anomaly, combined into a single scalar via a learned linear head trained to predict human-annotated topological event timestamps — this is low-overhead at inference time and could be calibrated per-scene-type, analogous to how change-point detection algorithms like BOCPD (Adams & MacKay, 2007) maintain a lightweight run-length posterior rather than full distributional state. The first critical failure mode of aggressive compression is aliasing across crisis types: occlusion, merging, and appearance discontinuity have qualitatively different implications for which corrective action is appropriate, but a scalar signal cannot distinguish them — triggering the same generic reset in response to all three will be actively harmful in cases where the right response differs, for instance a full slot re-bind is appropriate for occlusion but destructive for a lighting change where the binding is correct and only appearance needs updating. The second failure mode is adversarial smoothness: natural scenes can have topological crises that unfold gradually — a slow occlusion over 15 frames rather than a hard boundary — during which the per-frame surprise signal stays below threshold even though the cumulative binding damage is severe, essentially a slow drift that evades the spike detector entirely. Third and most subtly, a learned surprise signal trained on a fixed dataset will have domain-specific calibration: a model trained on driving video will learn that large optical flow near image boundaries signals occlusion, but this prior transfers poorly to tabletop manipulation or medical imaging where the statistical signature of topological events is entirely different, meaning the compression has baked in scene-class assumptions that are invisible until deployment on out-of-distribution content. The fundamental issue is that compressing topological surprise to a scalar requires choosing a sufficient statistic for binding crisis probability, and the no-free-lunch intuition applies: any fixed compression will be maximally informative for the crisis types that dominate the training distribution and systematically blind to rarer or structurally different crises, which are precisely the cases where a corrective mechanism is most needed.

A model can absolutely learn to steer away from topological boundaries during generation — this is essentially what conservative world models in RL do: Kidambi et al.'s MOPO and Yu et al.'s COMBO explicitly penalize transitions that enter low-confidence or high-uncertainty regions of the learned dynamics, and applied to video generation this would mean down-weighting predicted frames that the model's own uncertainty estimate flags as near a topological boundary. The steering mechanism is tractable: during beam search or diffusion sampling, you can add a topological stability reward to the sampling objective — penalizing candidate next-frames whose latent representation would cause high slot entropy or large slot velocity — effectively turning the surprise signal from a passive detector into an active repulsive potential in generation space, similar to how classifier-free guidance steers diffusion models but toward dynamical stability rather than semantic class. The fidelity implication is immediate and severe: topological boundaries are not optional features of video, they are load-bearing structure. Occlusions carry depth information; object merges signal physical interaction; appearance discontinuities mark illumination changes that ground scene understanding — a model that systematically avoids generating these events will produce video that is dynamically stable but physically lobotomized, with objects gliding past each other without occluding, scenes frozen in perpetual soft lighting, and interactions that never resolve into contact. Empirically this failure mode is already visible in long-rollout samples from models like TECO and MCVD, where extended generations show an increasing bias toward slow, smooth, low-event-rate dynamics — the model has implicitly learned that "safe" predictions are ones that stay near the high-density core of the training distribution, which for natural video means low-motion, low-occlusion scenes. The deeper implication is that stability and physical realism are in direct conflict for autoregressive video models in a way that has no clean resolution: the events that make video informationally rich are exactly the events that stress the model's binding architecture, so any training signal that rewards long-rollout coherence will simultaneously penalize the generation of physically meaningful interactions. This suggests the framing of "avoiding crises" is ultimately wrong — the right goal is not crisis avoidance but crisis recovery, which requires the model to have a robust re-initialization mechanism that can restore distributional fidelity after a topological event rather than steering around it.
